name: The Build Watcher
oneLiner: Triggers an ADO pipeline run and polls it to completion, returning a pass/fail verdict — no tab-refreshing to catch the result.
lead: Fire-and-forget CI/CD. This agent POSTs a pipeline run to the ADO REST API, polls its `state` on a fixed interval, and reports succeeded/failed the moment the run terminates. Build, test, or deploy pipelines — same flow.
chore: Kick off a pipeline, then keep flipping to a browser tab every few minutes to check if it's done. A run can take 30 minutes. Focus drifts, failures go unnoticed for an hour, and cancelling a hung run means hunting through the ADO UI for the stop button.
instead: The agent triggers the run, then polls `getRunStatus` every 30s until `state === 'completed'`, then prints the result, elapsed time, and run URL. On request it fetches published artifacts or PATCHes a stuck run to `canceling` — all headless.
whyItMatters: A failed build caught in seconds instead of an hour keeps the team from stacking work on a broken base.

howItWorks.step: Give it a pipeline ID and optionally a branch. It POSTs to `/pipelines/{id}/runs` on the ADO REST API (api-version 7.0), defaulting `refName` to `refs/heads/main`, and gets back a run ID to track.
howItWorks.explain: Triggering a run is a single **POST** to `/pipelines/{id}/runs` — ADO creates *and* queues the run in one call, so there is no separate 'start' step. The branch is pinned through `resources.repositories.self.refName` (the `self` repo is the pipeline's own YAML repo), which must be a **full git ref** — `refs/heads/main`, never a bare `main`; passing a bare name silently falls back to the pipeline's default branch. The returned `run.id` is the handle every later poll and cancel needs, and `run._links.web.href` is the browser URL ADO hands back so a human can open the run.

howItWorks.step: Polls `getRunStatus` on a fixed interval — 30s by default — until `state` reads `completed`, then reports the outcome: succeeded or failed, elapsed time, and the run URL.
howItWorks.explain: This is a bounded poll: it re-reads `getRunStatus` every `pollInterval` (30s default) and only stops when `run.state === 'completed'` — ADO's terminal state. Crucially, `state` and `result` are **separate fields**: `state` says *whether* the run finished, `result` says *how* — so a completed run maps to success only when `run.result === 'succeeded'` (it could equally be `failed` or `canceled`). The `while (Date.now() - startTime < timeout)` guard caps the wait at 30 min so a hung run can't block forever, and a null status from a transient API hiccup bails out immediately rather than looping on a dead handle.

howItWorks.step: On request, fetches the artifacts the run published.
howItWorks.explain: A `GET` on `/runs/{runId}/artifacts` lists what the run published. A non-OK response returns `[]` rather than throwing, so a run with no artifacts — or a permissions gap — degrades to an empty list instead of breaking the caller. Each entry is flattened to `name`/`size`/`downloadUrl`, where the URL comes from `artifact.signedContent.url`: a **short-lived signed link** ADO mints on demand, so it must be used promptly and never cached or stored.

howItWorks.step: PATCHes a still-running run to `canceling`, on request.
howItWorks.explain: Cancelling is a **PATCH** (a partial update of the existing run), not a POST — the URL targets the run itself, and the body sets only `{ state: 'canceling' }`. You are declaring **intent**: ADO tears the run down asynchronously, so it moves to `canceling` first and only later to a terminal `completed`/`canceled` — it does not stop instantly. The function reports success once the request is accepted, not once the run has actually wound down, so a follow-up poll is what confirms the teardown finished.

underHood.heading: Triggering the run
underHood.whenRuns: When you trigger a build, test, or deploy pipeline.
underHood.input: A pipeline ID and optional branch.
underHood.output: A POST to the ADO pipelines endpoint, returning a run ID.

underHood.heading: Polling for completion
underHood.whenRuns: Every 30s (or your chosen interval) while the run is in progress.
underHood.output: The run's current `state` — in progress, or completed with a `result`.

underHood.heading: Reporting the verdict
underHood.output: Succeeded or failed, elapsed time, and the run URL.

underHood.heading: Fetching artifacts
underHood.whenRuns: Only on request, after a successful run.
underHood.output: A list of published artifacts with names, sizes, and signed download URLs.

underHood.heading: Cancelling a run
underHood.output: A PATCH to the ADO REST API; the run moves to `canceling`.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Azure DevOps access and a **PAT** with pipeline read/execute scope.
The pipeline IDs you want to run — build, test, and/or deploy — from whoever owns your CI setup.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the engine that runs the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is TypeScript run under Node — a one-time per-machine install.

steps.label: Clone the agent and install its dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the agent's dependencies into `node_modules`.
steps.firstRun: Cold install — a minute or two.

steps.label: Set the target org, project, PAT, and pipeline IDs (env vars).
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
export ADO_BUILD_PIPELINE_ID=123
export ADO_TEST_PIPELINE_ID=124
export ADO_DEPLOY_PIPELINE_ID=125
steps.why: Read at startup: which ADO org/project to hit, the PAT that authorizes it, and which pipeline ID maps to build/test/deploy. Nothing is hard-coded — swap these to point at another project.

steps.label: Trigger a run and poll it.
steps.cmd:
npm run ado:pipeline -- trigger 123 --branch main
# note the run number it prints, e.g. "Run #4821", then:
npm run ado:pipeline -- wait 123 4821
steps.why: `trigger` starts the run and returns its ID; `wait` polls that run every 30s until it reports succeeded or failed.
steps.firstRun: Triggers a fresh run and polls it end to end.
steps.rerun: Each `trigger` starts a new run with its own ID — never reused.

steps.label: Read the printed verdict.
steps.cmd:
# no file to open — the result prints straight to the terminal, e.g.:
# { "success": true, "data": { "runId": 4821, "result": "succeeded", "url": "..." } }
steps.why: No report file is written — the output is the immediate succeeded/failed verdict plus the run URL, printed straight to stdout.

inputs.name: trigger <pipeline-id> [--branch <name>]
inputs.desc: Triggers a run of the pipeline on the given branch (defaults to `main`).

inputs.name: wait <pipeline-id> <run-id>
inputs.desc: Polls a run every 30s until `completed`, then reports succeeded/failed.

inputs.name: environment variables
inputs.desc: Target ADO org/project, the PAT, and the pipeline IDs for build/test/deploy.

outputs.name: console verdict
outputs.desc: Succeeded or failed, run duration, and the run URL — printed to stdout, not persisted.

outputs.name: artifact list (on request)
outputs.desc: Names, sizes, and signed download URLs of the artifacts a successful run published.

runbook.rerun: No stored state — every `trigger` is a fresh run with its own ID. Re-running on the same branch just starts the pipeline over, which is exactly what you want after pushing a fix.
runbook.integrate: Wire the `trigger` + `wait` pair into whatever kicks off your CI/CD flow (a pre-merge gate, a nightly build) so no one refreshes a status page — the agent reports back the moment there's a verdict.

video.caption: A 2-3 minute screen recording: trigger a pipeline run and watch the agent report the verdict.
script: Open a terminal beside the team's shared to-do board in a browser, so viewers can compare.
Say: 'Normally you'd keep refreshing this page. Watch what this agent does instead.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's already done).
Show the `export ADO_...` lines; say 'this is the only place project-specific details live.'
Run `npm run ado:pipeline -- trigger 123 --branch main`; point out the run number it prints.
Run `npm run ado:pipeline -- wait 123 <run-id>`; narrate the 'state: inProgress... waiting' lines.
When it completes, read the printed verdict out loud — succeeded/failed, duration, link.
Briefly show `cancel` on a hypothetical stuck run — say when you'd use it.
Close: 'No one had to sit and watch a screen for that.'
